transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-29
Start time: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~61 minutes
Attendees: Amelia Chen (Redwood AE); Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE); Priya Nair (EmberWave Head of ML); Carlos Mendes (EmberWave Platform Eng); Leah Brooks (EmberWave CTO); Omar Aziz (EmberWave Data Scientist)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Quick POC scoping focused on unit economics: per-token estimates, batching/caching knobs, bench plan and timeline. Customer constraints: $15k/month pilot budget, strict 200ms p50 target for short responses, want canary in prod after pilot. Next: share bench harness, traffic trace, pricing options.

Topics:
- Workload sizing: conversational chat + retrieval-augmented generation + embedding calls
- Success criteria: latency SLOs, cost per 1M tokens, quality/regression thresholds
- Benchmarks: latency p50/p95, throughput QPS, cold/warm KV-cache cases
- Timeline: 2-week bench, 3-week pilot, canary rollout
- Budget constraints and batching tradeoffs

Transcript:
[00:00] Amelia: Alright everyone thanks for joining, um this is Amelia from Redwood. Diego and I will run through the POC scoping—try to keep it practical, um what you want to validate.
[00:12] Priya: Hi, thanks. We've been evaluating a couple vendors and really want to land on cost model and a realistic bench plan before exec sign-off. We're targetting a pilot budget of roughly $15k a month and want to know what that actually buys.
[00:24] Diego: Great, that's super helpful. Maybe to start can you describe the workload mix? like percent chat versus bulk embeddings and average response size?
[00:31] Carlos: Sure, approximate split: 65% conversational chat (avg user turn 300–600 tokens), 25% RAG summarization calls (document context pushes to 1.5k tokens), 10% embeddings (batch jobs at off-peak). Peak QPS currently ~12, sustained 4–6.
[00:48] Priya: Also important: 30% of chat requests are short replies (<= 60 tokens) and have a strict latency sLO — we want p50 < 200ms and p95 < 700ms ideally.
[01:04] Amelia: Okay that's very clear. Two levers we'll focus on: batching and prefix/KV caching. Batching increases throughput but can add latency for short replies; caching reduces token compute for repeated prefixes or system prompt. We'll propose a mixed policy — low-latency lane for short chat and batched lane for long generations.
[01:22] Leah: Can you translate that into unit economics? like per-token cost numbers so the finance team can do math.
[01:29] Diego: Yep. Quick back-of-envelope from our last runs — depending on model variant and quantization, per-token compute cost (GPU time amortized) ranges 0.0006–0.0020 USD per generated token for a 7B-class model on dedicated capacity. With batching and KV cache we often see effective per-token drop by 20–60% for repeat prefixes. For embeddings the unit cost looks different — embeddings per call are more expensive per token but done in batch so amortizes.
[01:53] Omar: Sorry can I interrupt: those numbers, are they for hosted or dedicated?
[01:56] Diego: Good question. Those numbers assume Redwood Dedicated with reserved capacity pricing; hosted API SKU will have slightly higher per-token list price but no infra ops. We will send a matrix of hosted vs dedicated vs private with delta.
[02:08] Priya: We need worst-case and expected-case numbers. Finance wants to assume no KV cache in worst case.
[02:15] Amelia: Yes. We'll produce a three-scenario table: worst (no cache, minimal batching), expected (some caching, opportunistic batching), and best (aggressive batching + warm caches + quantized model).
[02:26] Carlos: For the bench, we want concrete tests: p50/p95 latency for short replies, cold-start token throughput, and steady-state with warm KV cache. Also we'll want token-level cost estimations per million tokens.
[02:38] Diego: We'll define bench cases:
- Case A: short-convo synthetic trace (<=60 tokens) — measure p50/p95, record batching-induced latency
- Case B: long-gen RAG (1.5k context, 300–800 generated tokens) — measure throughput and cost per generated token
- Case C: embeddings batch job at 10k items — cost and time to completion
- Case D: mixed real trace replay — to validate routing policy and economic model

[03:05] Priya: Timeline? how long would it take to get bench results we can show to execs?
[03:09] Amelia: Two weeks for initial bench runs if we get the traffic trace and prompt set this week. Then a 3-week pilot to test canary in your staging/prod-like infra and verify cost numbers in the wild. So about 5 weeks total to a production canary.
[03:21] Leah: Our constraints: security/compliance review will add time — we need SSO/SAML + audit logs. Also KMS for keys since some data is regulated.
[03:31] Diego: That aligns with Redwood Private/Dedicated options; we can provide SOC2 docs and KMS integration checklist. We will include audit log forwarder and SAML/SCIM notes in the deliverables.
[03:41] Priya: Great. On batching knobs — can you explain how you decide batch windows? we saw other vendors using adaptive batching but wanted to understand practical knobs for p50-sensitive traffic.
[03:50] Diego: Sure. We use a two-lane approach: an 'immediate' lane with small or zero batching for short-turn requests (aiming to keep added batching latency <20ms), and a 'throughput' lane that waits up to X ms or Y requests before flushing. X and Y are knobs — e.g., 8–16 ms window and batch size cap of 16 for GPUs with low-latency kernels. For very latency-sensitive requests we prefer KV-cache warm paths so the actual per-token compute is much lower.
[04:18] Carlos: Is KV cache compatible with our sharded retrieval? we sometimes stitch prefixes with doc IDs.
[04:23] Diego: Yes, KV cache primarily helps with repeated prefixes and system prompts. For RAG where each context is unique we'll rely on batching and shorter decoder paths; we can also recommend quantized model variants to save compute on long gens.
[04:36] Amelia: On the finance front, Diego will prepare a per-token projection with three scenarios and show how batching + cache change effective cost per 1M tokens. We'll also include an example calc using your traffic split and the $15k budget to show what QPS / tokens per month that buys.
[04:52] Priya: That calc will be crucial. In worst-case (no cache) we need to understand how quickly costs could blow past $15k.
[04:58] Diego: We'll do a sensitivity table — breakpoints where cost exceeds budget. We'll also recommend throttling and lightweight LLM responses for low-value requests to stay within budget.
[05:10] Omar: For bench environment, do you need us to spin up anything on our side or can we run entirely against Redwood hosted endpoints?
[05:16] Amelia: We can run against hosted to start — less infra lift. If you want Dedicated-level numbers we recommend a short Dedicated staging instance so kernel selection and GPU perf reflect your target environment. We'll document the delta between hosted and dedicated.
[05:29] Leah: Security — send us your SOC2 and a data flow diagram. We have to run that by legal before any data leaves our VPC.
[05:36] Amelia: Will do. Diego, we'll attach the security pack and a redacted bench harness example.
[05:41] Diego: Yep. Also note: for embeddings we often recommend batching 256–1024 items per request to reduce per-item cost. For the embedding batch job we can estimate time-to-complete given your current throughput targets.
[05:53] Priya: On quality/regression — how do you propose we measure quality variance when we change quantization or model variants?
[05:59] Diego: We'll run an evaluation set — holdout prompt sets and automated metric gauges (ROUGE, BLEU-ish for summarization, embedding distance thresholds for retrieval accuracy) plus a small human A/B test. We'll tie regression alerts to the eval harness so the pilot flags if quality drops more than X points.
[06:14] Priya: Sounds good. Anything else on the bench config?
[06:17] Diego: We'll also capture tokenization overhead, token multipliers for long context (we'll log prompt vs generated tokens), and cold-start penalties (first request per process). These matter for p95.
[06:28] Amelia: Ok quick recap and next steps — Amelia doing the pricing sheet and bench plan, Diego builds the per-token matrix and bench config, Carlos uploads traffic traces, Priya confirms success criteria. We'll aim to reconvene after bench results — target 2026-12-14 for a results review.
[06:45] Leah: That date works, pending legal.
[06:47] Priya: Thanks, one more ask — can you include a simple runbook for cost controls (rate limits, fallback to smaller models, caching TTLs)?
[06:55] Amelia: Absolutely. We'll include concrete knobs and suggested default TTLs.
[06:59] Carlos: Thanks all.
[07:00] Amelia: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the repo link and schedule the workshop.

End of transcript.
